title: Broadening the reflection band of atomic mirrors by engineering the emitter-waveguide coupling
authors: C. -Y. Lee, G. -D. Lin, H. H. Jen, K. -T. Lin
abstract: We theoretically investigate single-photon coherent transport through a finite waveguide quantum electrodynamics (QED) array with spatially modulated emitter-waveguide couplings. By combining exact scattering calculations with spectral factorization and a semiclassical WKB analysis, we identify how the coupling profile controls the reflection bandwidth and its finite-size dependence. A Gaussian transverse displacement produces an exponential-of-Gaussian decay-rate profile that broadens the high-reflectivity window and suppresses the boundary-induced Fabry-Perot oscillations compared with a uniform array. The transmission zeros remain exactly degenerate at the atomic resonance for arbitrary positive coupling profiles at non-Bragg spacings. In contrast, the collective poles reorganize under the spatial modulation, redistributing their radiative widths and preventing individual subradiant resonances from terminating the reflection window. We further derive an algebraic 1/N scaling law for the contraction of the bandwidth toward its bulk value. The bulk bandwidth is determined by the largest local decay rate, whereas the finite-size correction increases as the profile becomes sharper, leading to an optimal profile width. These results establish spatial coupling engineering as a practical tool for designing broadband atomic mirrors in atom-nanofiber and circuit-QED platforms.
summary: This theoretical work demonstrates how tailoring the spatial coupling between emitters and a waveguide can engineer atomic mirrors to achieve broadband reflection. By implementing a Gaussian coupling profile, the paper shows that boundary-induced spectral limitations are overcome, leading to a much wider and flatter high-reflectivity window. This establishes spatial coupling engineering as a practical tool for advanced quantum photonic device design.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of broadening the reflection band of atomic mirrors, which is typically limited by boundary effects in finite arrays.
main_result: By engineering the emitter-waveguide coupling profile (e.g., using Gaussian transverse displacements), the reflection bandwidth can be significantly broadened, suppressing unwanted Fabry-Perot oscillations.
method: The study combines exact scattering calculations with spectral factorization and a semiclassical WKB analysis applied to an effective non-Hermitian Hamiltonian.
model_or_system: The system is a finite waveguide Quantum Electrodynamics (QED) array of two-level emitters coupled to a 1D waveguide. The physics is modeled using an effective non-Hermitian Hamiltonian in the single-excitation subspace.
key_observables: Reflection bandwidth, transmission zeros, collective poles, and the finite-size scaling of the bandwidth.
important_parameters: The coupling profile width ($\sigma$), the number of emitters ($N$), and the interatomic phase ($\varphi_0$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the rotating-wave approximation, linearizes photon dispersion, and neglects propagation delay across the array.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the reflection spectrum $|r|^2$ versus detuning ($\Delta$) for different coupling strengths, showing the transition from oscillatory behavior to a broad plateau.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the physical system and Hamiltonian, to applying advanced scattering formalisms, demonstrating the effect of coupling engineering on the spectrum, and finally deriving the finite-size scaling law for the bandwidth.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, controllable mechanism—spatial coupling engineering—to overcome fundamental limitations in designing high-performance photonic structures like atomic mirrors, which is highly relevant to quantum optics and open quantum systems.

N two-level emitters are coupled to a bidirectional 1D waveguide with uniform interatomic spacing d along the propagation axis (z axis). The local spontaneous decay rates γ j are modulated by tailored transverse displacements of the emitters relative to the waveguide axis. Because the guided mode is evanescent in the transverse direction, such displacements modify the local coupling strength exponentially.
